title: GWAS: Contingency Tables and Chi-Square
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter looks at how a genome-wide association study (GWAS) turns genotype data from a case-control cohort into a statistical claim that a variant is linked to a phenotype: how the data is laid out as a contingency table, and how that table is tested for association. It assumes the reader already has the basic vocabulary — what a SNP, an allele and a genotype are, and what a case-control study is. The source slide deck runs to sixty-odd pages, but the text layer used to build this chapter breaks off in the middle of the first worked example, right inside the chi-square formula; everything after that survives only as uncaptioned images (listed under Sources), so this chapter covers only the opening third of the lecture — the framing of the problem, the allele-frequency spectrum, and one contingency table carried through to a test statistic. No transcript, notes or problem set were supplied alongside the slides. ## Two ways to get the genotypes A GWAS starts from a cohort split into **cases** (people with the phenotype) and **controls** (people without it), and asks whether any variant's frequency differs between the two groups. The lecture names two ways of getting the genotype data to test: - **Allelic counts from SNP arrays** — variants are called from microarray data, one call per variant per individual. - **Read counts from sequencing** — multiple reads per variant per individual, so the count at a site is a depth of coverage rather than a single call. Once an association is found, the next step named on the slides is to **prioritize variants by estimated importance** — the slide deck states this as a goal for the lecture but the surviving text does not say how the prioritization is done. ## An association is not a cause The third point in the lecture's stated narrative is a warning: correlation between a variant and a phenotype is not the same thing as that variant causing the phenotype. The slides state this as a reason follow-up confirmation matters, without going further into how that confirmation is done in the material that survives here. ## What this lecture sets aside The slides explicitly flag three complications as out of scope for this lecture: 1. Non-random genotyping failure. 2. Population stratification, and how to correct for it. 3. Structural variants and copy-number variation. These are named as things a real GWAS analysis has to handle, but the lecture does not treat them here. ## The allele-frequency spectrum Before setting up the statistical test, the lecture places variants on a frequency spectrum, and pairs each band with the technology that was used to find it and the kind of trait it tends to explain: - **Around 50%** — high-frequency polymorphisms, the kind catalogued by HapMap and detectable on first-generation SNP arrays. - **Around 5%** — lower-frequency polymorphisms (the slide's examples are *CFTR* $\Delta$508 and *PCSK9* C679X), found via the 1000 Genomes Project and newer arrays with imputation. - **0.5% and below** — rare mutations, mostly the ones behind single-gene (Mendelian) traits (the slide's examples are *MC4R*, *ABCA1*, and 1q21.1 in schizophrenia), found by direct sequencing or by array-based detection of copy-number variants. The heuristic tying these bands together, stated directly on the slide, is **rarer alleles, stronger effects**: as a variant becomes rarer, it tends to carry a larger effect on the phenotype, and Mendelian traits — caused by a single gene — sit at the rare, strong-effect end of that spectrum. That trade-off is also why the technology changes band to band: a common variant shows up in a few hundred genotyped samples, but finding a rare one with confidence needs deeper sequencing or a purpose-built assay for structural variation. The lecture also showed an animation (credited to Itsik Pe'er, Columbia) illustrating cases and controls diverging over time; the animation itself is not captured in this conversion, only the label "Time $\longrightarrow$" that introduced it. ## Contingency tables: cases against controls at one locus The basic comparison is a **contingency table**: rows for the two values a variant can take at a locus, columns for case status, cells for counts. The slides name two versions of this: - An **allelic association test** tallies alleles. Since a person carries two alleles at an autosomal locus, each individual contributes two counts to the table — one per chromosome — so a cohort of $n$ people contributes $2n$ allele counts split between the two possible alleles. - A **genotypic association test** tallies people, not alleles: each individual is one of three genotypes (homozygous for either allele, or heterozygous), giving a $2 \times 3$ table of genotype against case status. The worked example that survives in the slides is the allelic version. ## Worked example: age-related macular degeneration The cohort: 2172 unrelated individuals of European descent, all at least 60 years old, collected at a time (2004, per the slide) when little was known about what caused age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Of these, 934 were controls with normal vision and 1238 were cases with AMD. At a single SNP, rs1061170, each of the 2172 individuals contributes two allele counts, for $2 \times 2172 = 4344$ allele observations in total — matching the grand total in the table below. Labelling the four cells $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ as the slide does: | Allele | Cases (with AMD) | Controls (without AMD) | Total | | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | C | 1522 ($a$) | 670 ($b$) | 2192 | | T | 954 ($c$) | 1198 ($d$) | 2152 | | **Total** | **2476** | **1868** | **4344** | If the C/T split were the same in cases and controls, the C allele's share of cases and of controls would match; here 1522 of 2476 case alleles are C (about 61%) against 670 of 1868 control alleles (about 36%) — a large gap the test below turns into a number. ## Testing the table: the chi-square statistic The slide sets up a chi-square test on exactly this $2\times2$ table, but the conversion cuts off mid-formula after $\chi^2 = \frac{(ad-bc)^2}{\cdots}$. The standard form of that statistic for a $2\times2$ table with cell counts $a, b, c, d$, row totals $a+b$ and $c+d$, column totals $a+c$ and $b+d$, and grand total $N$, is $$\chi^2 = \frac{N(ad - bc)^2}{(a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)}.$$ The intuition: under the null hypothesis that allele and case status are independent, each cell's expected count is determined by the row and column totals alone, and $ad - bc$ measures how far the observed table is from that independence — it is exactly zero when the two ratios $a{:}b$ and $c{:}d$ agree. Squaring and dividing by the totals turns that deviation into a statistic that is large exactly when the row (allele) split differs sharply between cases and controls, and it is compared against a chi-square distribution with one degree of freedom. Plugging in the rs1061170 numbers ($a=1522$, $b=670$, $c=954$, $d=1198$, $N=4344$) gives $\chi^2 \approx 279$ — nowhere near the table one would expect if the C allele were equally common in cases and controls, and enough to reject independence overwhelmingly. (This computation is not preserved in the source; it follows from the table using the formula above.) ## Other tests named, not worked Two further methods are named in the lecture's list of computational approaches but no formula or example for them survives in this conversion: - **Fisher's exact test**, an alternative to the chi-square test for a contingency table. - **Likelihood-based tests of case/control posterior genotypes.** Both are listed alongside the chi-square/contingency-table approach as targets for the lecture; the slide material available here does not go further into either. ## Sources - Slides: `computational-biology/mit-ocw/7091j/lectures/20-slides.md` ("Analysis of Genome Wide Association Studies (GWAS)", Lecture 20, David K. Gifford, MIT 7.91J, Spring 2014) — all sections above (narrative arc, computational approaches, out-of-scope list, allele-frequency spectrum, the case/control framing, the AMD cohort and the rs1061170 table) come from this file. The file's own banner notes it was reconstructed by a model from a PDF with no text layer, that the prose is a paraphrase in places, and that every equation is unverified; the chi-square formula given here completes a fragment that breaks off in the source (see "Testing the table" above), and the numeric evaluation of it is this chapter's own arithmetic on the table's counts, not something preserved from the slide. - No transcript, lecture notes or problem set were supplied for this lecture. - The slide deck's remaining content (roughly the last two-thirds of its sixty pages, following the rs1061170 table) is represented in the source file only as a list of uncaptioned extracted images (`20-slides/figures/p0##-#.*`) with no accompanying text, and could not be used here. - The animation credited to "Itsik Pe'er, Columbia" and the photographs illustrating the AMD cases/controls, both mentioned on the slides, are not captured in the conversion.
